common_names.name: Thundërkali e kuqe anemonia e kuqe

documentation.range: A. equina mediterranea (=A. schmidti) is found primarily in the North Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea, including Macaronesia, Portugal and Cantabric. It is common and widespread in the Mediterranean (Ocaña  et al. 2005, Chintiroglou and den Hartog 1995, Badalamenti et al. 2011; Ben Abdallah et al. 2012, Çinar et al. 2014), and the Dardanelles Strait in the Sea of Marmara (B. Ozalt pers. obs. 2014).
documentation.population: It is a common species but little information is available about the population density of this species. Populations densities between 15 and 45 ind/m2 has been observed in the shallow waters on northern Alborán Sea (A. Terrón-Sigler 2015 unpublished data).
documentation.habitats:
It is a considerably versatile intertidal sea anemone. It is found attached to hard substrata, both in exposed and sheltered situations, from the upper to lower shore and rarely in subtidal areas to depths of around 20 m. It is highly adapted to the intertidal zone as it tolerates high temperatures and desiccation, it can survive completely submerged in water or completely out of the water, high up on shores. The beadlet anemone is also found in regions of variable salinity such as estuaries or in the little rills of fresh water that often occur on beaches at low water (Shick 1991).

This anemone is omnivorous suspension feeder that eats organic detritus found in the water column (Chintiroglou and Koukouras 1992). It is the only species of anemone to brood their young (viviparous reproduction). The anemone begins as a planktonic larval stage where it crawls out of its parent and is free in the ocean for a short period of time. After that, it enters the cavity of another sea anemone, male or female, and further develops. Once the juvenile anemone is ready to be "born", the "parent" anemone catapults the new individual through the water where it lands and subsequentially secures itself on solid, solitary substrate (Rostron and Rostron 1978, Shick 1991, Monteiro et al. 1997, Perrin et al. 1999). They can also reproduce asexually through parthenogenesis of vegetative growth (e.g., regeneration or basal laceration (Rostron and Rostron 1978, Shick 1991)

In the Mediterranean Sea, asexual reproduction by longitudinal fission has been documented only once, while sexual reproduction occurs regularly in most locations (Chomsky et al. 2009).
documentation.threats: Several studies have showed that this species possess morphological and physiological adaptations to environmental changes, which include some pollution from garbage dumping, untreated sewage inflow, land and river runoff, and atmospheric fallout from heavy traffic and various small-scale industries scattered in coastal areas (Ormond and Caldwell 1982, Gadelha et al. 2010). Its effects on the population are little understood.
documentation.measures: The species is widespread and appear in numerous Mediterranean protected areas. At present day, there is not enough information about the species to develop conservation proposals and even to judge if they are necessary.
documentation.use_trade: It has been found to have antibacterial properties which seem to function differently than other antibiotic properties found in animals. They seem to be able to fight bacterial infections without the use of an enzyme called lysozyme. The chemicals produced by the beadlet anemone could possibly be harnessed for use in medicine or conservation (protecting plants against foreign bacteria) (Hutton and Smith 1996).
documentation.rationale: This species is a widely distributed in the Mediterranean. It is primarily found in the intertidal zone, but occurs occasionally to 20 m. Although it may be impacted by anthropogenic impacts in the intertidal and shallow coastal region, it appears to be fairly resilient to such impacts. Therefore, it is assessed as Least Concern. However, more efforts are needed to know its complete distribution in the Mediterranean and its conservation status in the Mediterranean.
documentation.taxonomic_notes:
This species should be recognized as Actinia schmidti (Ocaña et al. 2005).


According Schmidt (1972) there were two Mediterranean forms of A. equina mediterranea, A. equina mediterranea form I and A. equina mediterranea form II; both are thereafter recognized as morphological variations of the species A. schmidti (see Monteiro et al., 1997).
